title: Kitchener graft
subtitle: Joining two sets of live stitches invisibly with the tapestry needle.
excerpt: Kitchener graft, also called grafting, joins two rows of live stitches using the tapestry needle to weave a new row of knit stitches between them. The result is a seamless, stretchy join used on sock toes, fingertip closures, and the underarm joins of top-down yoke sweaters.
sourceNotes: Kitchener stitch named after Horatio Kitchener (First World War sock-knitting campaigns). The grafting technique itself is documented in Weldon's Practical Knitter sock volumes and Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938). The four-step mantra is common British and American knitting instruction practice.
heroPrompt: Close-up of a tapestry needle weaving yarn between two sets of live stitches on knitting needles, creating an invisible join at the toe of a sock.

glossaryTerms.definition: A technique for joining two sets of live stitches using a tapestry needle, mimicking a row of knit stitches to produce a flat, invisible, stretchy seam.
Stitches that remain on the needle and have not been cast off. They can still be worked, grafted, or put on hold.

content.text: uses the tapestry needle threaded with working yarn to weave an extra row of stitches between two sets of

, producing a join that looks identical to a knitted row. The technique is essential for sock toes and fingertip closures, and is used for underarm joins in seamless top-down sweaters. The four-step mantra below is the conventional way to remember the sequence. Difficulty: intermediate.
Equal numbers of live stitches on two parallel needles, the stitches arranged with right sides facing out
A blunt tapestry needle threaded with a length of working yarn approximately four times the width of the join
Hold the two needles parallel, right sides facing out. The front needle holds one set of stitches; the back needle holds the other. Thread the tapestry needle with the working yarn.
Set-up, front needle: insert the tapestry needle into the first front stitch purlwise (as if to purl) and pull the yarn through, leaving the stitch on the needle.
Set-up, back needle: insert the tapestry needle into the first back stitch knitwise (as if to knit) and pull the yarn through, leaving the stitch on the needle.
Four-step repeat, front needle, step 1: insert knitwise and pull through, removing the stitch from the needle.
Four-step repeat, front needle, step 2: insert into the next front stitch purlwise and pull through, leaving the stitch on the needle.
Four-step repeat, back needle, step 3: insert purlwise and pull through, removing the stitch from the needle.
Four-step repeat, back needle, step 4: insert into the next back stitch knitwise and pull through, leaving the stitch on the needle.

Repeat steps 3-6 across the row until one stitch remains on each needle. Work the last two stitches: insert knitwise through the last front stitch and remove; insert purlwise through the last back stitch and remove. Secure the yarn end.

attrs.title: The mantra
attrs.body: Front needle: knit off, purl on. Back needle: purl off, knit on. Repeat until done. Say this quietly as you work each stitch until the sequence is automatic.

content.text: Kitchener graft closes the toe of socks knitted from the cuff down or from the toe up. It joins the underarm stitches in top-down seamless sweaters, and finishes the fingers of knitted gloves. Any pattern instruction that says 'graft remaining stitches together' means Kitchener graft.

items.symptom: The grafted row looks like a purl row on the right side
items.cause: The set-up steps were skipped, or the front and back needles were swapped
items.fix: Re-check orientation. The needle holding the stitches closest to you is the front needle. Always begin with the set-up steps before entering the main four-step repeat.

items.cause: The tapestry needle yarn was pulled too firmly after each stitch
items.fix: After threading each stitch, leave the tension slightly loose. Ease the yarn to match the surrounding row height before moving to the next stitch.

items.symptom: A hole appears in the grafted row
items.cause: A stitch was entered in the wrong direction or a step was missed
items.fix: Work slowly and say the mantra aloud. Place a stitch marker between every ten stitches so a mistake can be located and unpicked without redoing the whole join.

items.symptom: Unequal stitch counts on the two needles
items.cause: The last round of knitting distributed stitches unevenly
items.fix: Before grafting, re-distribute the stitches so each needle holds exactly the same number. Kitchener graft requires a one-to-one match.
